Immigration attitudes and trust in law enforcement aren't simple they're layered, intersectional, and deeply shaped by who we are and what we've experienced.

Full study here: jurnal.itscience.org/index.p…

For more data-driven analysis subscribe: austinkocher.substack.com

Media exposure matters too. People who closely follow political news tended to be slightly more open to immigration. But the effect was modest, suggesting political identity shapes how people interpret the news more than the news itself changes minds.

The study found that socioeconomic class alone did not significantly predict immigration preferences or law enforcement perceptions suggesting that race, education, and ideology are more powerful drivers than income bracket.

Younger respondents (ages 18–34) were more likely to support higher immigration levels than older age groups. Older respondents, by contrast, tended to view police more favorably, pointing to real generational differences on both issues.

People who believed immigration would take jobs away from current residents were significantly more likely to prefer lower immigration levels, showing how economic anxiety connects directly to immigration attitudes.
When local law enforcement collaborates with ICE, trust among undocumented immigrants in those agencies drops and that drop extends to beliefs about whether police will protect their rights at all.

Racial identity shaped law enforcement perceptions in a measurable way. The study found that Black respondents reported notably less favorable views of police, reflecting patterns consistent with historical and ongoing experiences of racial bias.
Perceptions of police brutality had a major effect on trust in law enforcement. People who believed police frequently use excessive force had significantly less favorable views of police overall.

Education also mattered significantly. The study found that as education levels increase, support for more restrictive immigration policies decreases, suggesting that higher education correlates with more openness toward immigration.

Political ideology was one of the strongest predictors in the study. People with more liberal ideologies were more likely to support higher immigration levels, while those with conservative views were more likely to prefer stricter immigration policies.

The study analyzed data from the 2020 American National Election Studies survey using multiple linear regression models to examine what drives attitudes toward immigration policy and perceptions of law enforcement.
Research shows that how Americans feel about immigration and police is shaped by race, education, political ideology, and lived experience. Here's what the data actually says. 🧵

I have been informed by a reliable source that another person has died in ICE custody, this one in Adelanto. If true, it would be the 14th detained death this year, the 43rd under the Trump II, and the 4th at Adelanto. I'll share more info as available at austinkocher.substack.com.

My colleague Michael Wriston covered this story in full for Project Saltbox. If you want to understand how community opposition to ICE detention facilities actually unfolds on the ground, this is essential reading.

HRR sent a formal letter calling for a full public town hall to follow the closed session. Whether officials respond will say a lot about who this process is actually designed to serve.
This pattern is worth paying attention to. Grassroots groups do the organizing work that forces officials to respond, then get sidelined when formal conversations happen.

A Moore staffer had told HRR directly they would get a seat. When HRR followed up, they were told no. As HRR founder Patrick Dattilio put it: they're coming because of us, but they don't want us in the room.

On March 23, Gov. Wes Moore and Rep. April McClain Delaney held a closed roundtable in Hagerstown with "faith leaders, small businesses, and nonprofits." HRR (the group that drove public attention to this issue) was not invited.

Hagerstown Rapid Response (HRR) formed almost immediately after that report. They organized sustained opposition, protesting outside County Commissioner meetings where public comment had been suspended.

On Christmas Eve 2025, the Washington Post reported that the Trump administration was converting warehouses nationwide into immigration detention facilities and Williamsport, MD was among the targets.

A grassroots group in Maryland helped expose a $102.4M federal ICE detention facility. Then officials held a closed-door meeting about it and didn't invite them. This is a story about who gets a seat at the table. 🧵
Remember, someone dies every 6 days in a US detention facility. Learn the data, engage with it, share this thread, and demand a say over how your tax dollars are used.
Humanrightsfirst.org lets you track deportation and transfer flights of our detained population.

www.projectsaltbox.com features two very cool dudes who search through deeds and property info to track the land and warehouse space that ICE buys for future detention sites. From them we learn that ICE has spent 1 billion taxpayer dollars to create 40,000 beds so far.
Detentiondeaths.com is another outstanding citizen scholarship project tracking who has died in custody.  Of course, it cannot track those who are ill or injured, released, and die shortly after.
Detentionpregnancytracker.com tracks the pregnant women taken by ICE and what happens to them.
Enforcementdashboard.com is another great interface for some of this data.

Deportationdata.org is a project out of Berkeley that allows you to visualize data coming directly out of DHS own intake & processing systems. It isn't cleaned or interpreted, it's a by-product of immigration enforcement.

First check out detentionreports.com
to see how his team has leveraged FOIA to get the very best picture of what's going on.
